content.title: About
content.content: Kidney beans are large, meaty beans with a bright red color, belonging to the species Phaseolus vulgaris. They are widely used in many cuisines, especially in tomato‑based dishes, chili, salads, and stews. The beans are rich in protein, complex carbohydrates, and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name "kidney" comes from the bean’s shape, which resembles a human kidney.
More than 30 varieties of kidney beans exist, differing in size and shade of red.
Raw beans contain phytohemagglutinin, a toxic protein that is destroyed by proper cooking.
In the United States, kidney beans are a staple ingredient in chili con carne.
Soaking beans overnight speeds up cooking and improves nutrient absorption.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked kidney beans provides about 15 g of protein, making it valuable for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: High dietary fiber content
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are essential for blood formation and anemia prevention, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Low glycemic index after cooking
items.content: Cooked beans raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Kidney beans contain polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Toxicity of raw beans
items.content: Raw kidney beans contain phytohemagglutinin, which can cause severe food poisoning. Cook beans at a rolling boil for at least 10 minutes to destroy the toxin.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans may cause flatulence due to oligosaccharides; soaking and discarding the soaking water can reduce this effect.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to legumes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kidney beans are best enjoyed after boiling or stewing. Add them to chili, stews, salads, soups, or blend into a bean dip. They can also replace chickpeas in hummus recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 1 year. Cooked beans keep in the refrigerator for 4‑5 days or can be frozen in portion‑size bags.
